timeline.line: This is Marco Villanueva. He lashes containers at Mirsal Terminals in Abu Dhabi. His daughter Bea is seven, lives in Iloilo, and tells her class that her dad ties ships to the sea.
It's six in the evening before a hot night. Daniel plans the roster. His brief leads with three decisions, not thirty charts.
One click scores tomorrow night's roster. One hundred and sixty six people on graded work.
A hundred and nine fit. Fifty four fit with controls. Three to reassign. Three is the limit, so nobody cries wolf.
Marco is one of the three. Third night in a row, short sleep, a refresher not done, broken coolers in his camp block, and thirty five degrees forecast.
Every number is shown, layer by layer. The planner sees work reasons. Never a diagnosis, and never his group.
Seventy percent of tonight's risk is the shift itself: heat, night and the camp. Crew rules show where whole gangs are stretched.
Daniel accepts the swap. Ground twist-lock handling, same crew. Marco keeps his mates and loses the ladder.
Daniel asks the copilot a question. It answers only from what a planner may see.
Then he asks for Marco's lab results. It says no, politely. Some answers belong to the clinic.
The activity register shows each job's hazards, hours, safe working practice, and how well its controls held.
Behavioural groups explain patterns across twenty people or more. Never one person, and never origin or language.
Khalid, the shift manager, approves. The planner proposes, the manager approves. Two people, one log.
Next morning, Layla, the head of safety, sees Camp Block C in warning. Heat visits at the clinic and cooling faults rose together.
Each warning becomes a record. Here is what moved, against the camp's own baseline.
The copilot drafts, Layla confirms. Nothing counts until a person signs it.
She asks for the drivers section. Drafted in seconds, read, and signed.
One click builds the inspection: one check per driver, where and when it matters.
Then a real action. Fix eleven coolers, with an owner and a date to check it worked. Not a newsletter.
Six in the evening. Marco's phone explains the change in Filipino. His language, his reason.
One tap shows it in English, for the rest of us.
Check-in is three taps. Slept six to seven hours. Feeling good. Water, yes. Bea would approve.
He spots a loose ladder rung and reports it in one line. The copilot turns it into a proper record.
Safety cards come from confirmed lessons, short enough to read on the bus.
Priya issues permits. The warning hands her one section to sign: which permits carry the camp's conditions.
Each permit shows crew readiness as counts. Never names.
She accepts the warning's conditions, assesses the permit, and signs it.
Seven o'clock. Shift start. Work begins.
The roster scores again. Kiran didn't check in, so he's unknown, not fit. No data is not good news.
At Berth 2 the deck sensor stays above thirty two for half an hour. Joseph, the foreman, gets one clear change: rest, shade and water. One tap.
Sunita feels unwell. Two taps, and the clinic knows.
The permit log says a crew member went to the cool room. It doesn't say who. That's on purpose.
At her desk, Layla confirms Marco's ladder report. Now it counts in the job's safety history.
The lesson is drafted, signed, and shared with the crews who need it.
Does any of this work? On ninety days of history it caught four of four events, at least seventy four hours early.
Switch the clinic feed off and you see exactly what you lose. No silent gaps.
The impact calculator runs on your numbers, not ours.
Sara, the clinician, sees the health detail and has the final word: fit, with restrictions.
Marco decides whether his employer sees that outcome. He shares it. His call.
The authority sees district totals. Small groups stay hidden. Privacy is the default, not a setting.
Every draft and every decision lands in an audit trail nobody can edit. Not even Layla. She checked.
Governance shows who sees what, the privacy threshold, and model weights that change only when a person approves.
Every feed shows how fresh it is. Late is named, not guessed. A new feed connects from a spreadsheet.
Hessa, the admin, onboards a new foreman in under a minute.
Morning. The warning closes as right. That's how lead time and false alarms get measured.
And at one in the afternoon in Iloilo, Bea gets her video call. Dad's tired. Dad's fine. Dad's home in August. That's the whole point.
